clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase, the enzyme that hydrolyses S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) to homocysteine and adenosine
In contrast to the benign hypermethioninaemias, this is a treatable disorder with real risk of neurological and hepatic disease if missed
Accumulated SAH inhibits many methyltransferases, so hypermethioninaemia occurs together with raised SAH and often raised S-adenosylmethionine
Typical features are hypotonia, myopathy with elevated creatine kinase, developmental delay and hepatic dysfunction
A markedly elevated SAH is the discriminating biochemical finding compared with MAT I/III and GNMT deficiency
May be detected through hypermethioninaemia on newborn screening, prompting confirmatory testing
Fetal or neonatal presentations with coagulopathy and severe hepatopathy have been described
Management is generic: a methionine-restricted diet with supplementation such as creatine and phosphatidylcholine to support methylation-dependent pathways
reference.pathophysiology: S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase removes S-adenosylhomocysteine, the product formed whenever S-adenosylmethionine donates a methyl group. Because SAH is a potent feedback inhibitor of methyltransferases, its clearance is essential to keep transmethylation running. When the enzyme is deficient, SAH accumulates and inhibits methylation reactions throughout the body, while methionine and S-adenosylmethionine also rise as the cycle backs up. Impaired methylation, particularly of substrates important for muscle and liver, together with disturbed creatine and phosphatidylcholine synthesis, is thought to produce the myopathy, hepatopathy and neurodevelopmental features.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal or infantile liver disease of other cause with raised methionine
Primary myopathies with raised creatine kinase
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids demonstrating raised methionine
Creatine kinase and liver function tests including coagulation
Brain MRI where neurological features are present
redFlags: Developmental regression suggesting untreated methylation failure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on early recognition and treatment; dietary and supplementary therapy can improve muscle, liver and developmental outcomes, whereas late diagnosis carries a risk of persistent neurological and hepatic impairment.
pitfalls: Dismissing hypermethioninaemia as benign without measuring SAH, thereby missing this treatable disorder
Attributing the raised creatine kinase to a primary muscle disease
Mistaking the neonatal hepatopathy for another cause of infantile liver failure
Failing to distinguish it from MAT I/III and GNMT deficiency, which have very different implications
references: Baric I et al. S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency
